utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al., thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, Accused Popovic and Beara are absent for today. Mr. Zivanovic do we have a waiver?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will provide it very soon and we can proceed without Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The same goes for us as well. We've spoken to our client and the waiver should be coming shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. Ostojic. Representation, it's Prosecution the same as last week. Defence teams I notice of absence of Mr. Bourgon, and that's it, I think. Witness Momir Popovic -- Nikolic is present this morning already, and he's assisted by counsel, Mr. Tansey. All right. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I hope you've been able to rest over the weekend so that we can take it up where we left off last week.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I reviewed the transcript, and since we had a couple of speedy exchanges, would I like to put several questions to you in order to clarify certain ambiguities in the transcript. Before I move on to the questions I put to you, at transcript pages 3182 and 83, in response to Mr. Ostojic's questions you talked about the chaos that reigned in the town between the 11th and 13th of July, 1995, and you described the situation in great detail by saying that there was general chaos, that the situation in relation to the status of prisoners was horrific, that decisions changed by not the hour but by half an hour, in fact. I will not go on to the read the entire page. If I understood you correctly, the decisions taken were inconsistent and contradictory and there was general confusion around. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can agree with such an assertion, yes. Just tell me what particular matters are you referring to when you say that there were contradictory decisions? At least two or three elements were engaged in the whole operation. I said that what was lacking was a continuity of decisions. What I was able to see: Along one line of the MUP, one sort of instructions were passed down; along the other line, which was that of the military, was still other; and the third one, I'm merely trying to separate them so that everything is clear. The third line was the political decisions, the decision taken by the political structures. That's what I meant when I said that there was lack of continuity and inconsistency in these decisions. That's what I had primarily in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that's how I understood it, that there was general confusion without any definite plan of action. Before I go back to the other issues which had to do with your alleged stay in Zvornik, you will recall my learned friends asking you about the conversations you had with the OTP just prior to your pleading guilty. It was the 28th and 29th of April and the 1st of May, 2003. You spoke of a manner of matters including volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I need to raise the name of a person, I would like us to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means Ms. Nikolic. Let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On Friday, Mr. Nikolic, we completed our discussion concerning your alleged arrival in Zvornik. You said that you did not announce your imminent arrival to the Zvornik Brigade, and nobody expected your arrival on the evening of the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the reception booth when you registered with your personal details, as you testified last Friday, did you see whether the duty policeman in the reception booth phoned the command at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever details I give you now could not accurately reflect what happened. I can only retell this in two or three sentences. I came to the reception booth. I asked that I be allowed to get in touch with Mr. Drago Nikolic. I provided my ID, and I explained already what sort of ID that was. One of the individuals who were in the reception booth accompanied me upstairs, and that's all I can tell you, all the details I can provide you with. Madam Nikolic, let me just tell you this: Had I taken it upon myself to memorise all the details, including the individual who was in the reception booth, the individual who accompanied me to the headquarters, and the individual who I found in the office there, I would have done so. On that particular day, I saw hundreds of new faces, new soldiers, new officers. Believe me that this was not a priority of mine. I did not pay attention to that. He was simply a soldier who took me where I wanted to go. I didn't pay attention to his appearance, his age, et cetera. I had this one particular task which I had to convey to Drago Nikolic and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words you don't know and you don't recall whether the duty officer did place a telephone call or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, please slow down a little bit, please. You're jumping straight with your question before the witness has even finished his answer. And you, please, Mr. Nikolic, do the same for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Thank you, Your Honours, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise. I will try to make a pause before I answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On Friday at page 33224, line 9 for the benefit of my learned friends, you said you that you did not even attempt to enter the grounds of the Zvornik Brigade with your car. Why? It is quite customary for the officers to park with their car right in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I remember that particular detail, the gate was closed. I first pulled over right outside there, and then I went on to park -- and again don't hold me to these details. It is almost 15 years later now that we're discussing these matters. I think I parked right across from the barracks where there's like a sort of a lay-by that I could use to park my car, and then I got into the headquarters on foot. I don't know why. I told you already, Madam Nikolic, that I simply don't remember the details because I did not find them significant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You also said that you could not remember the individual who accompanied you from the gate to the headquarters building.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, but I do believe you can distinguish between a military policeman and an ordinary soldier. Do the policemen have any special insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military policemen have military belts that are different from those worn by other soldiers, but to my mind he was simply a uniformed person accompanying me. Was he really a military policeman who was a member of the Zvornik Brigade military police, or was he an individual employed at the gate? In the Bratunac Brigade we did not have military policemen manning the reception booth. I suppose that he was an individual tasked with the duties relating to the reception booth to maintain communication between his command and the individuals coming to visit. I really did not find it relevant. In my view, though, he -- or, rather, I think he was a member of the military police, which of course need not be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Nikolic. At least up here we do have a problem in that we are not receiving the transcript on LiveNote. It's scrolling on the main monitor but not on LiveNote. If there are no objections we will proceed, and then in the meantime our technicians will work towards fixing the problem. I hear no objections. We will proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no problem with proceeding, Your Honours. At the stage where I will be needing a document from e-court, we could deal with that by using hard copies rather than stopping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, I don't think that will be a problem, because that's -- I don't see that that part of the system is affected as yet. What's affected only is the transcript on -- on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. However, when e-court appears on my middle screen, then I no longer can see the transcript, which of course poses a problem for my work, but we'll see as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I'd like to go back to you visiting the Zvornik Brigade. You said that a number of soldiers remained in and around the reception booth, and you said exactly how many there were on Friday. Did they follow you when you set out toward the HQ building with that particular soldier, or did they stay behind?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was only accompanied by that particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The other ones stayed behind, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were or what they were tasked with. I only saw them there as a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the witness, I would like now to call 3D498, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, shortly you will see a photograph in front of you. Do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One -- one moment, Mr. Nikolic. Ms. Nikolic and all your colleagues, including the Prosecution, I am informed that there is a complete crash of the e-court system in all the building. So -- yes, but how did he get it? I don't have it. Yes, but Judge Stole has it. All right. Can we use a hard copy, please? If we have -- we should have one. Now Judge Prost has it as well. All right. Okay. All right. You can see it if you go on LiveNote, the e-court where we get copies of the images, et cetera. There you can see it. Yes, Ms. Nikolic. If you could proceed, please. The accused can't see it. Well, we need a hard copy. Do we have one handy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can see it. I have the photograph in front of me. I can see the buildings and the car that Ms. Nikolic wants to point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the problem, Mr. Nikolic. It's -- let's proceed with a hard copy that we can show to the accused at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see this on the ELMO, because none of my screens is showing that everything is okay. I hope the accused have it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you recognise this photograph and what's depicted in it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise this photograph because I see it for the first time. However, it depicts the buildings that, again, I assume are the buildings that belonged to the Zvornik Brigade command HQ, but again I'm not sure. I seen only one of the buildings of the Zvornik Brigade where I went during the war, and after the war I told you how many times I went there. As for the surrounding of the buildings, this picture is something that simply doesn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is this the Zvornik Brigade command building?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should have taken the picture of the whole section of the town in order to ask me that. Last time I told you where I went exactly. As for making recognitions on the basis of the photographs, I don't want to make any guesswork. You have three buildings in this photograph, and I can only suppose -- or I can tell you exactly which building I entered. However, among these three buildings I cannot tell you exactly because they all look alike to me. I didn't pay any attention, and I don't know how the building looked like and what was around it. I can tell you where I went and which office I visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind to do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I told Mr. Zivanovic last time I will tell to you again to you. I same to the reception booth. It's on the right-hand side. And then I took -- went straight away, and after a minute or two minutes, I don't know what the distance was, you have to turn left and then you climb the stairs into the building. This is the best to my -- my recollection. I went on a floor. I took a flight of stairs -- or two, actually, flight of stairs. There was a landing, and if I remember correctly, we entered an office which is a little bit diagonally to the left from the landing, and this is the best I can remember. What was there actually, Ms. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you further questions. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. This is what I remember best. As for the identification of the buildings from this photograph, I really cannot do that 15 years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you cannot confirm that this is the Zvornik Brigade command building based on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is. All these buildings of the Zvornik Brigade command HQ are similar to these ones. They looked like prefabricated buildings, and that's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another photograph. Maybe it will be easier to refresh your memory on the basis of that photograph. Can we please now look at 3D497. This is the -- the reception booth, and behind it, if you can see it, there's a building. Does this photograph help you to recollect the route that you took, that you described a minute ago from the reception booth to the building?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This reception booth is what we see here on the right-hand side of the photograph. Now, can I mark this with a ball-point pen, the route that I took?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if you enter from the road and you get to the reception booth, this is this control point or check-point, as far as I can remember. Then one proceeds this way, makes a -- makes a turn, and approximately this entrance that I'm just showing you, to the best of my recollection --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Nikolic. I think that Mr. Thayer has stood up particularly for this purpose. Can you please do this on this hard copy on the ELMO, because if you are making marks on the screens the other people in the courtroom cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this here is the reception booth, and this is where I talked to the people who were inside. After everything that took place that I already told you, I went this way, behind the reception booth, and as far as I can remember and what I can see in this photograph, this is approximately the command building, and this is the door that I went through.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the date on this paper and your signature.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask the usher to show to the witness the Exhibit 3D110.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before the usher comes back, we can go back to this exhibit. In the meantime, I'll ask you a few questions. According to your statement of facts, 4D16, item 10, you said that together with this policeman you had gone to look for the duty officer, and the two of you went into the office of the duty -- the duty officer. That's what you testified.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You told to the duty officer that you were looking for Drago Nikolic. Was that the first time that you heard that Drago Nikolic was at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How many men were in the room of the duty officer when you entered?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man who met us, that is the duty officer, this military policeman, and myself. Later on, we were joined by another individual who was called to come into this office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look the ELMO in front of you. You will see the layout. That's e-court page 2. This is the first floor of the Zvornik Brigade HQ. This is the layout of the whole building. So could you kindly mark the room of the duty operations officer, where you found this man.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I honestly don't want to speculate and guess. I cannot read this layout, because I'm not an expert. I don't know. This doesn't mean anything to me. I cannot comprehend this layout, and I don't want to make any marks about anything that I don't understand. Therefore, whatever I mark, in my view, means nothing. I don't know how to work with this kind of layout or plans or -- therefore, I'm not prepared to make any marks. Quite simply, I cannot find my way around this layout. It's all the same to me. And I'm not ready or prepared to mark any marks about something that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A minute ago, Mr. Nikolic, you explained to us in every detail that you climbed the stairs. Anyone can see the stairs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Please. You're making the interpreters' lives difficult. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If someone is leading me or escorting me who knows how to read this layout, I can try to explain to you. If this is the staircase, and I'm not sure, probably is, I can really only guess. So if this is the staircase and you climb the stairs to the first floor and then you arrive at the landing, and this is the landing and these are the rooms. So to the best of my recollection, the room that I entered after I climbed the stairs was diagonally to the light -- to the right -- to the left, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to insist. Can you please just put the date and your signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, those who would like to try and reconnect the LiveNote, it seems that the transcript is ready now and available. And it's up-to-date. In other words, what was missing before has been filled in, but you have to reconnect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In this office of the duty operations officer, after reading the transcript in the Blagojevic case, you had to wait for a while for another officer to arrive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That individual appeared, did he? And then what happened? Who was that man who joined you? Did he address you? Did he ask if he could help you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I had a feeling, but I'm not sure, that he was from the same organ that Drago Nikolic belonged to. He asked me if he could be of any help. I told him that what I need to convey or pursuant to the order that I had received would be to convey directly to Mr. Drago Nikolic, and that was generally what we discussed. After that, I was told that Drago Nikolic was at the IKM and that if that was the case somebody would escort me to the IKM. Actually, the same person who escorted me from the reception booth. That would be, in short, what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on what did you conclude, Mr. Nikolic, that this officer was from the intelligence and security sector, the sector that Mr. Drago Nikolic belonged to? Only Mr. Trbic was there, and you said that you had never seen him before according to your testimony in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my testimony. I had never seen Trbic before, and all I testified to was correct. Now, on the basis of what did I reach the conclusion that he was from the same sector? Well, that seemed to be the most reasonable explanation to me. They had to call someone who was knowledgeable about these things, but if you ask me that would be someone from the same sector. Even if I was in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the security sector there was no one else but Drago Nikolic and Mr. Trbic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was engaged in the security sector. I don't know how many there were or who they were in addition to Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Based on everything you've told us and described for us, your stay in the Zvornik Brigade, by the time you parked your car, went through the gate, got into the HQ building, and then got back to your car, all of that must have taken at least 20 minutes to half an hour. You'll agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long it took me to do all that, but not long, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, sometime after 10.00 you set out for the forward command post with the military policeman who was assigned to be your escort; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set out once I finished all this business at the brigade headquarters. I didn't have a watch on me, and I didn't know the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you engage in any conversation at all with the military policeman while you were in the car? Did he introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. We must have talked about something, but nothing of any consequence that I would remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: According to your earlier testimony in the Blagojevic case and according to the statement of facts, you said that you -- that the road you travelled was very poor, that it was a macadam road, a dirt road, and that it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by all I stated then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The road was quite narrow, full of bends, and going uphill and downhill, and you said that you took some 40 minutes to reach the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road was partly a dirt road. Not right away, but after you leave the brigade HQ and that particular area. It was in poor condition. It was a dirt road. It was not an asphalt road. I told you roughly how long it took us to get there. I don't know if that was indeed the case. I can't be more precise, or precise, in fact, how long it took us to reach the IKM from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In your statement of facts, 4D16, at paragraph 10 you specified that it was 45 minutes. Can you please repeat your answer? We don't have it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said at the time, roughly 45 minutes, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you reached the forward command post, did anyone stop you or check you, anyone from the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the road to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, most of us went to the forward command post, and you will agree with me it is on top of a hill; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there once, and I know that that was where I found Drago Nikolic, that that was the forward command post. Whether it was a hill or a valley. I arrived there in the evening hours. As I said a moment ago, all the details you're asking me about were not something that I thought was relevant. I did not pay particular attention to the surroundings and to all the minor details you're asking me about. I can confirm that I reached the command -- forward command post, that nobody stopped me on the way, and the rest I told when I was answering Mr. Zivanovic's questions, and I confirm whatever I said now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you observe any other vehicles parked at the command -- forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I turned my vehicle, no, not at the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there soldiers at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any. When I was there, it seems -- or it's not that it seems to me. There was no one there when I got there. There may have been individuals in the building or around it, but where -- in the area where I saw Drago Nikolic, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Blagojevic case six years ago at page 2289, at lines 17 to 23, for the benefit of my learned friends, you stated that you entered the building where the brigade's IKM was housed and that that was where you finally found Drago Nikolic. Do you recall stating this in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I entered the building. I don't think that I said anything of the sort. I did state that I was outside the building. I never said that I got in. It may have been misinterpretation or something else. On the occasion of that visit I did not get into the IKM building. I stayed outside where we talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I will read out what you answered to the question of Mr. Stojanovic. Page 28 -- 2289, lines 15 through 21. "[In English] Only just managed to turn the car around where I had to do so, and it was just -- and it was just a house. Whether it was a holiday home or not, I really don't know. I just went inside that house." [Interpretation] This is what you stated in the Blagojevic case, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what the transcript reads, I have no reason to doubt what you say. I will seize the opportunity to correct that. I may have said as much. I apologise, but I know now, as I did then, that I did not linger there or go into the house, and I confirm this again. I did not enter the house. I did not linger in the house. The conversation took place outside. If I said so, I apologise and I correct it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wasn't your memory fresher in 2003 when you testified for the first time before a Chamber in the Blagojevic case than it is today? Would not your testimony given at the time be more reflective of the truth than what you're stating today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you the truth. I do not wish to deny that my memory was fresher six years ago than it is today. However, I'm telling you what really happened, and you can accept it or not. Again, I allow for the possibility that I misspoke and made a mistake when I was giving my statement at the time. My apologies. I don't think that I ever testified since that I entered the house and that I had my conversation with Drago Nikolic in the house. I don't recall a single such statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What I read out to you was your testimony in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe you, that I may have said something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let me remind you of something else that you stated in the Blagojevic case. When asked whether you saw a communications officer at the IKM, do you recall what your answer was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I answered that I heard that there were communications devices on the premises and that there were some individuals who had something to do with it. I don't think that I said anything in particular. I even believe that one of the individuals appeared in the doorway without actually coming out. That's the best of my recollection 15 years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was the house a smaller or a larger structure?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was a house by the macadam or dirt road, roughly to the right-hand side of the road as one travels toward the house. It had several steps leading to the front door of the house. How big or small was it, well, really, I know only the bit that I saw as I entered the yard. If I remember well, I passed the courtyard gate typical of the rural houses. I drove my car in reverse into the yard in order for me to be able to leave it then. That's the best of my recollection related to the house. I only saw the part where the front gate and door were, and I can't tell you how big or small the house was itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that it was to the right-hand side of the direction -- of the road in the direction you were travelling.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, yes. It was night-time, and that's what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If we take stock of the time based on your earlier testimonies and your testimony today and of the events you went through, you spoke -- you allegedly spoke with Drago Nikolic at the IKM roughly at 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not keep track of the time myself. I testified about talking to him. As for the time, I told your learned friends, too, that I tried to do my best and describe the time line. Was I precise enough? That's something I cannot really assess at the time. I tried to be as precise as possible, and I tried to describe the events. Everything I said was something that I could remember best.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely what I wanted to ask you about. If you reached the Zvornik Brigade at 2245 hours, as you said in your statement of facts, and then you spent some 15 to 20 minutes in the brigade before the whole procedure of your impending journey was resolved, and if it took you some 45 minutes to reach the IKM, then it leads us to some 2300 hours that you must have reached the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: -- IKM?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a correction for the record, Mr. President. In section 10 Mr. Nikolic's statement of facts, to which my friend is referring, it's written that he reached the Zvornik Brigade headquarters at around 21 -- 2145 hours, not 2245 hours. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Thayer. Do you agree, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I misspoke. 2145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nikolic, is everything clear in your mind? Can you proceed with your reply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to be quite correct and clear in what I'm saying. I do not wish to speculate about time, and I've said that countless times. Was it 15 minutes earlier or half an hour earlier or later, that's something I don't want to be hold -- held to. I'm not stating that I could fully pinpoint the exact time of day. That was roughly based on how I remember things happened. I do allow for the possibility that it may have happened 15 minutes or half an hour earlier or later. Really, I do not exclude the possibility that I may have made a mistake in assessing the exact time and the events as they happened at different intervals. Mr. Prosecutor did intervene, and he was correct that it was an hour earlier than suggested by you in your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer was really right to correct me. Otherwise, it would mean that you would reach the IKM at midnight, and my question was actually based on your statement of facts.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, I -- sorry, I tried to tell you what I think about the time line and the things that you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this conversation could have taken place quarter to 11.00, 11.00, or quarter past 11.00 on the 13th of July 1995. Let us wrap up this topic. I have information that you are a civil engineer and technician by profession?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I finished the secondary civil engineer's school.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The IKM, was that a solid-built house? Was it probably damaged by shells? Do you recall these details?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that question. I already told you what I noticed when I arrived there. Anything beyond that would be just making up things. I explained to you precisely what I saw the moment I arrived there approximately at the time that you have mentioned. I didn't pay any attention whether this was a solid-built house, what kind of structure it was. I really didn't pay any attention. I still don't know what kind of material it was built of.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday when you testified, you said that you had left the IKM with the military policeman who had escorted you there. After this reported conversation -- purported conversation with Mr. Drago Nikolic and that Mr. Drago Nikolic had remained at the IKM. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On your way back to towards the Zvornik Brigade down this dirt road, did you meet any vehicles coming from the opposite direction towards the IKM? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you testified earlier about your journey from Bratunac to Zvornik, you told us that you saw buses on the road. Do you perhaps remember when and where that was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the road leading from Zvornik to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see P2110 -- excuse me. P2111 in the e-court. P2111. It's a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this document, Mr. Nikolic, I'm going to tell you briefly that this is a map where the roads are marked, the roads that you took. This is the map indicating only one section of the road, not all the way to Zvornik. Could you please be so kind to tell us at which point you saw the buses and at what time while you were travelling reportedly to Zvornik and back?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Konjevic Polje. In fact, the cross-section --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Intersection in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if this is the road leading to Zvornik, and I assume that that's the case, it goes towards Drinjaca via Kuslat. Since we don't see these places in the map, I have to tell you that I saw the buses somewhere between Drinjaca. If this is Drinjaca here, if this is Drinjaca, I don't know exactly, but if this is Drinjaca, then it would be between Drinjaca and Konjevic Polje, in that section. This is the Konjevic Polje intersection, the road leading to Zvornik. This is Drinjaca. So that would be that on this section of the road I saw buses travelling towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Nikolic, write the word "bus "next to the arrow so that we can know in which direction these buses were moving.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- or under the assumption that this is the road leading to Zvornik, and they were travelling towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Can you please tell us at what time that happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was at the time when I was on my way back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was on the night of the 13th of July, 1995, after 2300 hours?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after I -- or, actually, while I was returning from Zvornik to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please put today's date on this document and your signature.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall not need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you remember how many buses were in this convoy, one or two?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned a convoy. I spoke about buses, individual buses, and that is what I saw. There was no convoy, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How many buses did you see?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I didn't count them. I saw a couple of buses travelling in that direction. There was no column or a large number of buses that were passing. Two, three at the most, but please don't hold me to that. I saw the buses passing. I didn't count them. I didn't particularly pay any attention to how many buses there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At Drinjaca-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road and the roundabout road that goes around Drina are converging there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the road leading from Konjevic Polje to Zvornik and from the Bratunac direction along the Drina, this is where these roads converge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said yourself, when you testified last Friday, that on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road there were a lot of patrols. According to the evidence, this road was closed for traffic or -- of buses or any other non-military vehicles. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. You probably have some documents or maybe you have seen an order to that effect, but the actual situation on that road was ... I myself travelled down this road, and it's not true that the road was closed on that evening. I do believe that at one point there was some check-points put on the road, and the units that were performing those tasks were rotated. But as for the rest, all the traffic went unhindered along this road, and that is all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you see at Drinjaca a column of six buses parked and with their headlights on?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: PW-169 witness testified before this court, and he said that a six-bus convoy was parked by the Drina with the prisoners and that the buses had their headlights on, and that was on the road that converges at the point where Drinjaca, and you say that you didn't see that column.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can say whatever he wants.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, my question was did you see that or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You interrupted his -- his answer. Let him finish. If it's not relevant we'll strike it off, but let him finish his answer first, please. Thank you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really want the situation to be perfectly clear. When I returned from Zvornik, members of the MP and their commander told me that the military policemen who were deployed on the bridge over the Drina, that was the joint patrol of the border police and the military police, that they had informed the commander that on the evening of the 13th, down the road which runs along the Drina, some buses had set off towards Zvornik with the Muslims who had been previously in Bratunac. Now, this is what I can confirm as my knowledge about the movement of these vehicles, but I personally didn't see them. This is probably the buses that had travelled down the Drina River and were stopped there. Since I am familiar with this area, they could have been stopped at Drinjaca before they took to the main road -- or, rather, the road that I travelled down and from where I would have been able to see them. Therefore, I can only confirm that according to the information that I received, a convoy of buses travelled along the Drina River, and what I saw with my own eyes is the buses that I previously mentioned that were travelling from Konjevic Polje to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we just go back for a moment to the Zvornik Brigade HQ and the duty operations officer room. Do you remember, did this officer register your visit at the time and your request to meet with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really have to ask the duty operations officer. I don't know what the procedure was in place in the Zvornik Brigade, and I wasn't interested in that at all, whether he registered my name. It wasn't my business to take care of that. I simply didn't pay attention, and I really cannot answer your question. Whether he was supposed to register my name or not, I don't know what the procedure, what the standard procedure of the Zvornik Brigade was. I don't know if he wrote down my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As for the standard procedure in the Zvornik Brigade, was to record all the messages and all the visits by officers by other units, and this has been entered --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the name -- the date and the number of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, you're kindly asked to repeat the name and the page of the book, please, date and number of the book. Name, date, number of the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise again to the interpreters. This was duty operations officer log-book, Exhibit Number P377, and the standard procedure was to enter the names of the visitors.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't finished. Your name appears -- actually, appears not to have been recorded on the 13th of July. The duty operations officer, on the 13th of July, 1995, was Sreten Milosevic. In the interview he gave to the OTP, he never mentioned your visit, and this is what Sreten Milosevic told us on the 27th of April, 2007, actually, to the investigators of the Defence: "On the 13th of July, 1995, I was duty operations officer at the Zvornik Brigade command HQ. All the individuals who were not part of the Zvornik Brigade command but who came to see me during my shift were registered in the duty operations officer's logbook. If someone's name is not entered, then this person never came. I do not remember Momir Nikolic, and I know who he is, but I wasn't acquainted with him, had come looking for Drago Nikolic, nor was anyone was assigned to accompany him to the Kitovnica IKM. I honestly don't remember any such event." This is what Sreten Milosevic stated about his shift as a duty operations officer regarding the 13th of July when you allegedly went to the Zvornik Brigade command. This is what he responded to our questions. You yourself don't remember any details. You don't remember the policemen or their names, and according to the duty operations officer's statement and the entries for the 13th of July, 1995, Mr. Nikolic, you were not at the Zvornik Brigade command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I -- I do respect the gentleman gave his statement. Of course, we all know and you say that -- what you say, that the practice was for everyone who visited to have been recorded. I myself am aware of a different practice that was in existence. I don't know whether it was in accordance with the standing rules of procedure, but this is what the practice was: In the corps command, security organs were never recorded. They were never disarmed. In other words, I was never disarmed, and I visited the corps command to see the corps commander, let's say General Zivanovic. I don't know that I was ever registered. I never produced any ID I had on me. I introduced myself as a security organ, and I was never subject to they subsequent checks, registration, or anything of the sort. Probably the Zvornik Brigade had a different practice of procedure, but I'm telling you that there were other practices in place as well. If the gentleman who was the duty officer didn't -- wasn't acquainted with me, how could he have then stated that I wasn't there in the first place? I don't have the entire witness's statement in front of me. What I can tell you is that I went to the Zvornik Brigade, and I did as much as I related. I don't want to take up your time any more. I repeat that I was in the Zvornik Brigade to -- there to convey the order I got from Mr. Beara, and I state that today as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I'll take more than five minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, but we need to have the break now. Thank you. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have several questions for you still. Please have patience. In the course of your today's testimony, pages -- page 21, lines 21 to 22, you said that when you were at the IKM you said the following: "I believe that one of the individuals," and you meant the communications officers, "appeared in the doorway without stepping outside." Do you recall where exactly it was that the individual was standing in the house?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was in the doorway of the front door. Drago Nikolic got out of the house, and he stood in the doorway which was to my left, if I recall correctly. He came to the door, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was there a patio or were there any steps in front of the door?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were steps, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the man who stopped at the door as you were approaching the house?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered the question. I said that I don't want to speculate or describe persons I saw at a glance for some 30 seconds and only once in my life. He wore a uniform, and -- as well as everybody else, and they all looked alike. I don't want to speculate. That's why I'm asking you not to ask me to describe him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And he must have been standing on the top of the stairs and must have been in a higher position compared to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you where he stood.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you suppose that he was a communications officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, please, and allow for a pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You assumed that he was a communications officer on duty together with Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Be patient, please. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, a communications officer testified before this Trial Chamber who was on duty with Drago Nikolic at the IKM on the 13th of July 2000 -- or, rather, it was on the 6th of September, 2009 that he testified, pages 21295, lines 10 to 13. In answer to the question whether on the 13th of July an officer came to the IKM, either from the Zvornik Brigade or any other unit, he said that nobody came. In view of this and the fact that you do not recall a multitude of details, in view of the fact that you positioned the house erroneously, and in view of the contrary evidence, throughout the period of time you were negotiating a plea agreement and you were giving a statement of facts, you were under a great deal of pressure, you wanted the agreement to come about, you will agree with me that one of the important topics that you discussed with the OTP was that you should provide them with details as to who decided when to send prisoners from Bratunac to -- to Zvornik, that you were told that unless you provided them with the details there would be no agreement with the OTP forthcoming. You were not either in the Zvornik Brigade [realtime transcript read in error "orally"] or at the IKM. You fabricated this story about your visit to HQ and to the IKM because you simply didn't have a choice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are your conclusions, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have need to answer the question you put to me. What you presented here is a conclusion of yours and you're entitled to that. The only point I want to make is that you do not have a single shred of evidence, and let me tell you that the OTP had never conditioned my agreement on me providing them information about Zvornik and the transfer of prisoners to Zvornik. It had never been conditioned upon my agreement. I claim that the OTP had never presented such a condition as you presented here, or any other condition. I stated in my previous evidence that as with every other negotiations there were problems and points where we disagreed, but unlike what you said, there was no blackmailing. I wasn't either blackmailed or compelled or conditioned by anything and induced into an agreement in this way. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you testified that you were under a great deal of pressure and that you wanted dearly for the agreement to come about. Let me just make a correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Don't overlap, please. You've been overlapping. Ms. Nikolic, if you could kindly proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to make a correction in the transcript. Page 34, line 15. I said he wasn't either at the Zvornik Brigade or at the IKM, and we have erroneously the word "orally" there. Can this be corrected. Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your last question was not recorded at all, as well as his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will repeat what we have here. You need to look at line 8 of page 35, madam. Mr. Nikolic, you testified that you were under a great deal of pressure and that you wanted dearly for the agreement to come about, and then you said something else, and he intervened. I don't know what he said. That's when I asked you to -- not to overlap, both of you, but in the meantime we don't know what else you said, and we don't know what Mr. Nikolic replied. So what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have anymore questions, Your Honour. That was my statement at the end. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- say that the relations I had with OTP concerning the negotiations and the pressure that Madam Nikolic referred to, all of these matters have been extensively discussed by me, and I have nothing to add on this score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next is the Borovcanin Defence team. Mr. Gosnell, if you could introduce yourself to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Chris Gosnell and I represent Mr. Borovcanin along with my colleagues here. I'm going to be asking you a few questions this morning. I will try to make these questions as clear and as focussed as possible, but by all means if there is anything that's vague or not clear, please let know and I'll do my best to clarify. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to start with Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic's role in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have P4482.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, coming up on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And page 31 in the English and page 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, what you see coming up on the screen in front you is an extract of your testimony in the Trbic case before the BiH State Court on the 1st of September, 2008. And here's what you say during that testimony: "Q. After what you saw and what you did in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995, did you tell Colonel Radoslav Jankovic about that? "A. There was no need for me to inform him given that Colonel Jankovic himself was deployed in Potocari. He was the one in charge, not myself. Colonel Jankovic was the one who established contacts, who took over all the affairs pertaining to security and intelligence that have to be performed by the Bratunac Brigade. Colonel Jankovic performed these activities on behalf of the Bratunac Brigade, presumably upon the order of the Main Staff. So there was nothing to communicate to him as he was the one in charge. He was the boss and the person in charge of everything." Now, first of all I want to ask you, sir, do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you confirm that indeed Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic was physically present in Potocari on the 12th of July while the evacuation and screening process was under way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this Chamber has heard testimony from a Dutch officer who said that he complained directly to Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic during this evacuation process on the 12th of July, and he complained about his officers not having access to the white house where detainees were being held. Did you ever hear or learn about Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic talking to DutchBat personnel about such issues during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer this question in the following way: As for the contacts and discussions of all matters related to the attitude of the VRS, and primarily I'm referring to the Bratunac Brigade, before Colonel Jankovic's arrival, in addition to my duties which were the duties of an security and intelligence officer, I also discharged the duties of communications officer, liaison officer, with DutchBat in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. Other people were in charge of other areas. Colonel Vukovic Vukota was for the Skelani Brigade, and for the Milici Brigade it was Major Sargic who was in charge, and he was part of the team negotiating on all the issues related to Srebrenica. With Colonel Jankovic's arrival, and this is something that I testified about before, he himself came to my office and said that he had orders from the Main Staff that in view of the seriousness of the situation and in view of what was to follow in the subsequent several days, that he would be taking over the duties that I discharged since I was only a Captain and a reserve officer at that. And among other things, he told me that all the subsequent contacts with DutchBat personnel and representatives of the international forces in Srebrenica would now come under his competence and that he would be the one to personally decide on these matters, schedule meetings, and everything else. Indeed this is how things happened. I'm telling you what I know. I can't talk about specific meetings and me having been present there to see these things happen. What I can confirm, though, is what you can find in a number of documents that I was able to see before the start of process. I can't give you the time line about me seeing Colonel Jankovic meeting with officers. I can't tell you the matters that they discussed. What I can confirm is that he was among the officers who independently took decisions, as far as I was able to see. He specifically decided about who he was going to meet with and when, and it is on that basis that you -- what -- what the basis from which his authorities and powers followed was something that I can't tell you. Presumably, he was conferred upon these powers by his superiors. I can tell you that he independently took decisions and scheduled meetings and decided on whatever he was asked to decide upon. That's what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. That's very helpful. And on that point let's bring up 4D726.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, just for my friends in the courtroom, this is actually an extract from Mr. Nikolic's testimony in Blagojevic, and we have simply put it into a separate document so that it will come up more quickly on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm sorry, we don't have this in B/C/S, but it's there on the screen in front you in English, and you were asked in this passage about Colonel Jankovic's authority over the evacuation of refugees, the basis for his authority, and you were asked specifically whether Jankovic could give you orders, and here's what you said in response, and this is at line 23 of transcript page 1920: "As I understood the rules and in view of the position held by Colonel Jankovic - so I'm answering your first question first - his arrival to the Bratunac Brigade and his visit to my office and his contacts and presence there created the conviction that he was a man from the Main Staff who can give me orders as to what I should do when it comes to the prisoners, the refugees, because generally speaking and as a rule, I knew and was aware even before receiving the order that concern for the refugees and the prisoners, their Assembly, their securing and transportation, was within the competence of the intelligence and security organ." Now, of course taking into account what you've said in your further statement of facts, I just want to ask you whether you would confirm this statement that you made in Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm this statement, and that was the impression I gained at the time, without any doubt. My position today of the role and the relations that prevailed at the time does not differ from what it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, last week during your testimony you said in response to a question from my learned friend from the Prosecution that you were not an expert in relation to matters concerning the MUP chain of command, but then you described your understanding that MUP forces in the area of the Zvornik Security Centre were under the authority of Dragomir Vasic, and we, to be clear, do not dispute that. But now I want to ask you specifically about the status of units assigned to Mr. Borovcanin. And could we please have on the screen 4D337. Now, sir, you were shown this document during your interview with Mr. McCloskey in May 2003. Do you remember him doing that, showing you this document during at that interview.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Could we now have on the screen P4472. And this is page 102 of the English, please, and page 104 of the B/C/S. Now, in English it's starting at the top of the page on line 1, and Mr. McCloskey is asking you about this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe the B/C/S needs to be scrolled down slightly to line 19, I believe, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, your answer in response to the query from Mr. McCloskey about the meaning of this document, you said, and I quote: "This means to me that the police forces under the command of Mr. Borovcanin, that they are coming into the area of responsibility of the Bratunac, that they are gonna be tasked with General Krstic, and they are being put under his command." Then Mr. McCloskey asks you: "Okay. Why can't this mean they are just working together as partners with General Krstic and the army? "A. But they usually work together, but it's logical that the commander of the operation is General Krstic, and it's logical that the police units are being put under the command of the military units in the field. "Q. Based on what? "A. It's defined by law. "Q. So it's more than just logical. It has a legal requirement. "A. Yes. There is a law that defines these relations." Now, sir, do you stand by what you answered Mr. McCloskey during that interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, given this authority that you've just described about Colonel Jankovic, and given this particular order and your interpretation of the order, would it be correct to say that Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic also had the authority to issue instructions to Dusko Jevic concerning how to carry out the process of evacuation in Potocari? I'm told that there might have been a slight mistranslation. Let me just repeat the question then in its totality. Given the authority that you described Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic having and given this order that we've just looked at and your interpretation thereof, would it be correct to say that Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic had the authority to issue instructions to Dusko Jevic as to how to carry out the process of evacuating people from Potocari on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try to tell you what my opinion is about this. I think that Colonel Jankovic, I don't know that, I don't know what kind of authorisation he had been given, that's not something that I know of, whether he received that from General Krstic or General Mladic and a what kind of powers that they conferred upon him, therefore I cannot confirm what you are asking me about, whether he could give orders, but given what I saw and what happened in Potocari, I personally think, but I reiterate once again that I'm not an expert in this area, I can only give you my personal opinion, which is that considering the relationship that existed between the police and the army, I think that Colonel Jankovic could tell Mr. Jevic or to suggest to him what to do and how to do it, and I think it's only natural. This kind of cooperation and this kind of relationship is only natural. However, I cannot talk about command relationship because I know nothing about that. Who is in command, who can issue orders to whom, I wouldn't like to guess about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I would now like to go on to a new topic and to go back to the 11th of July, 1995. And in your statement of facts and also your testimony last week, you've described that you were receiving intelligence information about what was going on in the enclave on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can we now have 4D692, please. Can we just have the B/C/S down in the bottom of the page, please, and then scroll it back up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, if you would like to have a look at a hard copy of any of these documents, we're very happy to provide one to you. Would that assist you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I can see this. It's important that I understand what the contents are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sure. And, sir, that is report or an information of some sort apparently from you addressed to the Drina Corps Command, specifically to the attention of General Krstic at the IKM, which we know was at Pribicevac, and this is dated the 11th of July, and the handwritten receipt seems to indicate that this document was received at 1350 hours on that day. Now, you've already testified last week about having prepared intelligence documents, reports, on this day. Do you remember having drafted or sent this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I see here, I cannot deduce that, but if you have this in a handwritten document, if possible, then I can decisively say whether this is something that I drafted or not. Or if I can look at the signature, because I'm not sure that this is my handwriting, but we can have a look at it provided you have a handwritten version of the document that I can be more precise in giving you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's fair enough, sir. Unfortunately, we don't have a handwritten version of this document. But in any event, I would just like to ask -- direct your attention to the middle of the page where it says: "Muslims are pulling out of Srebrenica towards Potocari, heading to Suceska, Milacivici, Pale. Command of the 28th Division has been moved to the village of Potocari. " Now, regardless of whether you actually prepared this document, I wonder whether you can tell us whether this is consistent with the information that you had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this -- excuse me. There was lots of information and reports that I was sending those days. I do not deny at all that I could have sent a report of this kind. I am not disputing that, but I don't remember. I think that either this is the first time that I see this document, or maybe I just forgotten about it. I sent out lots of information and reports, maybe several times a day on occasion. Therefore, I cannot remember specifically this information, because I wrote them all, being in the capacity of an intelligence and security organ. And, excuse me, one more thing. Provided I can see the handwriting, then I can say for sure that this was a report sent out by me as it is. But the content of this report is particularly something that pertains to that period and the events that took place in that period. I only have doubts about this statement that the command of the 28th Division was relocated to Potocari. I think that I personally would never have written something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could now have 4D693, please. Now, this appears to be a draft handwritten order for active combat operations from the Drina Corps Command, from the IKM at Pribicevac. It's not dated, but for the benefit of my friends in the courtroom, these two documents, the previous one and then this one, were found together on the EDS general collection, and they have sequential ERN numbers. And this is addressed to the Milici Brigade, and the first item says that: "The Milici Brigade is to take control of the village of Kutuzero." And the second item says: "Bratunac Brigade towards Milacevici." And it says that it is an order for active operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to ask you whether you saw this document at the time. I'd simply like to know whether you ever heard whether Bratunac Brigade forces were sent towards Milacevici, or did you hear about any other unit instead having been sent towards Milacevici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, is there any particular date that we're talking about or any time during this entire operation that may be more useful for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about the time period, so I first of all restrict it to the 12th and 13th. Let's start there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All Right. Let's [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Or, I'm sorry, perhaps I should also include the evening, late afternoon, evening, of the 11th, or the 12th and 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's clear enough for the time being. Mr. Nikolic, do you wish the question repeated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need. The question is clear to me, but I don't think I can say anything about this document, because I see it for the first time. I can see only one sheet in front of me. It doesn't tell me anything. In that period the Bratunac Brigade, and I'm talking exclusively about the Bratunac Brigade. I don't know nothing -- anything about the Milici Brigade. The Bratunac Brigade was engaged in that period but which orders it received and which tasks were given to it on which dates, except the one relating to Milacevici, I can't say anything further because I can't read anything from this document, and I can't be more specific. I know what the Bratunac Brigade and the battalions had as a task within the operation. This probably refers to the movement of units to -- I don't know really. I wouldn't like to comment on something that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. That's fair enough, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we now have 4D694, please, on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report from the head of the security and intelligence organ of the Milici Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Goran Kalvesic [phoen], and there on the first line -- and it's dated the 12th of July, addressed to the Drina Corps Security and Intelligence Department, and there in the first line it says: "On," and then there's an illegible word, "at about 1600 hours in the general area of Buljim, the following person detached from a group of soldiers that was moving from the direction of Srebrenica and surrendered to the VRS." Now, this document would seem to suggest that there were forces from the Milici Brigade around Ravni Buljim at this time. Did you ever hear about the presence of Milici Brigade forces in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The Milici Brigade, concerning the area that you are commencing, that is the Ravni Buljim sector was in direct contact with the forces of the Bratunac Brigade in this particular section. So if I remember correctly, or in Ravni Buljim or thereabouts is exactly where the zone of responsibility of the Milici Brigade begins; that is, from Bratunac towards Milici, and then from Ravni Buljim to Bratunac is the area of responsibility of the Milici Brigade. And this is the point of linking between the units of the Bratunac Brigade and units of the Milici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just to tie this up with a couple of additional documents, could we please have 4D695, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this appears, sir, to be a dispatch from the Milici Public Security Station, dated 12 July 1995. This document suggests that forces of the Milici Brigade were in contact with the Bosnian Muslim column in the area of Pobuda on 12 July, and that they were asking the Zvornik CJB for assistance in searching out these forces. Now, I realise that you probably didn't see this document, but I would like you to confirm it you can whether you ever heard about the presence of the Milici Brigade in the area of Pobuda at this time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't like to speak about something that I'm not familiar with. Whether they were in the area or not, I really don't know. I can confirm that this is the first time that I'm seeing this document. I am sure that I didn't have any direct information about their presence in this area, nor have I ever seen a document that would help me to conclude that they were definitely there. That is my answer. Of course, this area was also -- actually, it wasn't very close to them, but I do not rule out the possibility that they were deployed there. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
