utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just have one last document on this topic, and that is 4D697. Sir, can you focus your attention on -- well, this is a report, a daily combat report from the Milici Brigade to the Drina Corps command, dated 14 July 1995, and I'd like to address your attention to item 9. Now, again, probably you've never seen this document before and I understand that, but I'd like to ask you about the content of item 9, which says: "Continue with intense and organised search of the terrain with the aim to destroy the broken-up enemy groups in the depth of our territory and in the territory of the former enclave." Now, does this document in any way refresh your memory about whether or not there may have been combat going on in this area with forces of the Milici Brigade, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only try to deduce a logical conclusion, and I'm reluctant to do that. I have no knowledge. I didn't have any information about their being engaged in these tasks, and I know nothing about what the Milici Brigade was actually engaged in. I can only draw some conclusions on the basis of what I see in front of me, and I wouldn't like to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I wouldn't like you to do that either, sir, so thank you very much for your answer. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we now have the assistance of the usher to move a map near the witness. Now, this map is in e-court as P1504, but -- and we should call it up on the screen, please. But unfortunately the quality of scanning is fairly low, so it would be very difficult for those in the courtroom to follow, specifically some of the notations I'm going to go through the witness with, but let me assure you that we'll rescan it and have a version in e-court that is of a higher quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, what you have before you is a map, and it has a title which says: "Plan of Deployment of Drina Corps Forces to Prevent Enemy Forces from the enclaves Zepa and Srebrenica to Pass Towards Kladanj, Tuzla." The map is dated 1995, but there's no more specific date on it and it's not signed. Now, sir, do you remember at any time having seen this map before today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just have a few questions about some of the notations on the map, and I'd like to ask you if you can just assist us with what those notations are and what you think they might be describing. If you look closely at Srebrenica town and Potocari, you'll see a series of blue flags with writing. Can you tell us what that writing appears to be and what it designates, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These blue flags, as far as I can see in the map, indicates the command post -- posts of certain units. If I see it correctly. I don't see the numbers or designations, none of that, but these are command posts, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Command posts of which army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And if you look further north and find the junction of Konjevic Polje. Can you see that? You might, perhaps, need to move a little closer if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I stand up?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nikolic, because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course you were not speaking into the microphone and you were not listening to the interpretation because you did not have your headphones on. If you could tell us which part or what did you point to on the map when you were standing next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I pointed the direction, actually, Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, because the gentleman asked me about Konjevic Polje, and to look what is annotated where Konjevic Polje is. I got up. I found this road between Potocari-Bratunac via Konjevic Polje, and I looked at what is situated in the area around Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Sir, do you see a red flag situated near that intersection? Just for clarification, a red flag in that same area where the intersection is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only see one red flag, and I can show it to you in order to avoid any misunderstanding. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. And can you confirm that the notation there next to that flag indicates that elements of the 5th Engineering Battalion were located at that spot and elements of civilian police as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see on the map, an engineering unit was in Konjevic Polje. It says here the 5th Engineers Battalion. I know which unit it was. And also, there were MUP forces there -- or, rather, MUP units. That is as far as I know. It was not any particular MUP unit. It was a squad, although a squad is a unit, but they were manning this check-point which was held by the MUP. Excuse me. Just one more thing. And this squad, as far as I know, at that time was part of the Bratunac Public Security Station, the chief of which Mr. Miodrag Anovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, that MUP squad that you've just referred to, was that, to the best of your knowledge, more or less continuously at that location from March through July 1995, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I travelled along at that route. What I know for a fact is that it was a unit with a permanent task of manning the check-point. I don't know what their task specifically was, but it was a check-point in the area of Konjevic Polje, and they were members of the Bratunac Public Security Station, and they rotated on that check-point. So the personnel manning the check-point was not always the same. They rotated from among the ranks of the Bratunac Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, just a correction for the transcript. You identified the commander of the Bratunac public security station as Miodrag -- the transcript says Miodrag Stojanovic. Can you confirm that it's Miodrag Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Miodrag Josipovic was the chief of the Bratunac Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we have 4D651, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, this appears to be an order from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic, dated 10 July 1995, and the subject line is: "Order to Mobilise Men Liable for Military Service who are Engaged in Compulsory Work." And it says: "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS aimed at breaking the enemy offensive in the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipality areas I hereby order: "1. Fully mobilise all men liable for military service engaged in compulsory work by 1800 hours on 10 July..." Now, I'm not going to ask you, sir, whether you saw this order. I'm just going to ask whether you know this order was issued and implemented.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment. As you can see for yourself, the order was sent to the Ministry of Defence and archived. It wasn't sent to any other bodies or members of the brigade command. Consequently, I didn't see the order, but I do know that the forces -- or, rather, the persons referred to in this order were mobilised. All the able-bodied men who were engaged in work obligation were mobilised, and now I can see that it was pursuant to this order that the mobilisation I knew of was carried out. However, I didn't see the order itself. I may have seen it among the documents but did not pay much attention to it because it was not addressed to me, and it was not related to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. My name Ms. Natasha Fauveau Ivanovic and I represent General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions regarding the activities on the Bratunac Brigade on the Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 4D605, please. And while we're waiting for this document to be -- to appear on the screens --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: -- it's document that bears your name and the document bears the date of the 10th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need page 5 in B/C/S, please, and we have the right page in English, in fact. In this document we can see that it talks about the seizure of a vehicle that belonged to Medecins sans Frontieres, Doctors Without Borders, and this was something that was not told the coordination organ. This is a piece of equipment that was not reported to the coordination organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the document, and by what I can see, I am the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I'm particularly interested in with respect to this document is -- is the second paragraph in English, and in B/C/S it's line number 6, the sentence that begins with "By the request." [In English] "By the request one did not seek and the coordinating body did not approve import of plumbing-related material." [Interpretation] Were you able to find this excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I wanted to read through most of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the following: According to this document, it would appear that Doctors Without Borders tried to introduce into the enclave material for which it did not have authorisation. Is it true to say that international organisations, the various international organisations that would enter the enclave used humanitarian convoys and to bring material into Srebrenica, prohibited merchandise that was then used by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is something that I cannot agree with. There were isolated cases of violation in terms of what they held permission for. This is something that I do not dispute, and my attitude toward it was as it was. Whatever was not granted permission from the coordinating body and whatever was not entered into the accompanying documentation they had on them was something that I insisted should not get into Srebrenica. However, one cannot generalise the way you did. These were individual cases. What you said, that this was for military purposes, well, one can clearly say that this particular case involved plumbing material, and that's at least what I heard through interpretation. I apologise if this is wrong. Generally speaking, this was not an issue. There were individual cases. Whatever was not given permission for was taken away, was seized by those manning the check-point. Of course, only after they had consulted with the corps as to whether the material should be seized or not, as to what sort of status the material would be granted after it was seized. That's as much as I know about the work of the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit 5D955. This is an exhibit stemming from the army or, rather, the Ministry of Defence of BiH of Srebrenica. I imagine that you never saw this document previously. I would like you to read the document and pay particular attention to the last paragraph of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree now that some of the merchandise that would enter Srebrenica was used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... don't. I do not agree, because I am privy to all the details related to this. Where they say that some of this was received from the DutchBat does not in itself carry the meaning you confer upon it. The DutchBat -- DutchBat had a team which assisted both us, the civilians in Bratunac, and the civilians in Srebrenica. Let me be quite precise. I do not wish to assert that some of the provisions they gave them were not used for military purposes by those in Srebrenica, but likewise, the humanitarian aid given by DutchBat to the civilians in Bratunac was also partly used by us, the VRS. The DutchBat provided the humanitarian aid to the civilians both in Srebrenica and Bratunac. That much I can tell you. They had a team which was in charge of these issues only. I talked to them, and do you know what they told me in response? They wanted to accord equal treatment to all the population in Srebrenica and Bratunac and to appease the generally hostile atmosphere prevailing in the area. They wanted the people to see them as a party that had good intentions toward everyone. We discussed these matters quite often.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this document their is a mention of food. So DutchBat had sufficient amounts of food to also give or distribute to the enclave. They did not miss out on food.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can tell you is this, and I do have documents supporting this that I can show to you indicating that DutchBat personnel in this particular period of time, and I don't know what the situation was like other than through what they told me. I don't know what their food provisions were, but at the time, they had a very high dynamic of food supplies coming in from the territory or from a company that was in the territory of Bratunac. I have documents indicating in what way the supplies came through and what they consisted of in this particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: They had the approval of the competent organs of the Republika Srpska in order to get all this in Bratunac, and that was at the Hotel Fontana; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had all the permits from representatives of the civilian authorities, in other words, ministries that were competent for these matters. They had the permits from the military authorities, including the Main Staff and the Drina Corps, which detailed the needs to carry out checks of the goods, and they had also the necessary permits from their own HQ in Tuzla. That's what I know. I have the complete documentation about these matters with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The document that we just saw previously concerning -- about the material and the equipment that the MSF was trying to bring to Srebrenica mentioned a coordination organ. I would like to show you Exhibit 5D1437, and this is an approval from the coordination organ. Is it true to say that the Bratunac Brigade did not receive these approvals from the coordination organ, but the -- but it was sent by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing this sort of notification from the coordinating body. What we received were exhaustive lists of all the items that were supposed to enter the enclave within a particular convoy. They detailed the items and quantities involved, as well as the means of transport involved. I had never seen a certificate, receipt, or permission from -- bearing the signature of Mr. Dragan Kekic. I know who Dragan Kekic is. We received an order from the Main Staff via the Drina Corps on to specific brigades. In most of the cases, these documents were signed by General Milovanovic, the chief of staff. In certain cases there were names of the late Koljevic and Madam Biljana Plavsic there as well. They must have made up the coordinating body. However, in most of the cases the signature was of Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, tell us, is it true that no humanitarian convey from the UNPROFOR was able to go through the check-point in Zuti Most unless they had this information or this document from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. My apologies, or the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know when the check-point in Zuti Most was established? Approximately if you know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately after the setting up of the Srebrenica enclave. I don't know the exact date. There are documents bearing the exact date of its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you now document P2678. This is a document stemming from General Milovanovic. The document bears the date of the 2nd of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible to show point 3? It's at the very bottom of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As you can see here, we can see that an ICRC team was to enter Srebrenica on the 5th of April, 1995, and they were supposed to go back on the 8th of April, 1995, and return, actually, on the 8th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown page 3 on both languages. It's page 3 in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On this page, points 4 and 5 mention the MSF teams that were to enter into Srebrenica on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that all these convoys, before they would arrive to the check-point at Zuti Most, had to go through a check-point when they would enter on the territory of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, tell us, these convoys were checked at the first check-point when they would enter on the territory of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably. That's the information I had, that they were checked upon their entry into the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it not true to say that in Zuti Most all you had to do was to make sure that this was a convoy that was already announced without really making a detailed control of the merchandise it was carrying?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. My brigade commander set up -- or, rather, appointed a group of persons who were charged with doing this alone and at Zuti Most. Depending on the circumstances of a case, checks were carried out to make sure that the goods matched the supporting documentation insofar as the persons doing this deemed was necessary to do that. They wouldn't proceed to rummage through tons and tons of flour. There were individuals who had that particular job and did it based on their discretion. Had there been no need for a check-point to be manned at Zuti Most, then it would have been abolished by the brigade commander or the corps commander, or they would have issued instructions detailing in what other manner the convoys were to be checked. However, this was the procedure put in place in order to make sure that the convoys entering the area were indeed carrying what the specifications said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 4 of this document. According to what General Milovanovic wrote, it was -- what one had to do was to carry out the control and to ensure the movement of these convoys without any problems. Would you agree that the RCIC [as interpreted] teams, as well as MSF teams, were to enter Srebrenica without any problems after the control was established?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I agree. Once checks were carried out and if everything was found to match the accompanying documentation, they could proceed and carry on with their journey without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to go back to page 1 of the same document, please. We can see that there's a handwritten note. Do you know if you yourself wrote this note?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my note.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it your commander at the time? We see the name of Colonel Ognjenovic. Did he give you this instruction?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I can't claim with any certainty who it was who gave me the instruction, but I most definitely did not decide this of my own initiative. I was either told ordered to do that. This dates from 1994. In view of what the relations with Colonel Ognjenovic were at the time and his attitude toward the enclave and everything else, I can claim almost with certainty that it must have been a part of his order at the time, but I have no proof to back that. I'm sure that I did not take such decisions out of my own initiative, and I wasn't entitled to either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I am not trying to say that you made this up. However, what I would like to mention to you is that this order that you got from someone was not really corresponding to the instruction of the Main Staff which said that these convoys were to move unhindered through Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could accept that had there not been constant changes to this order. You know, just as I do, that no one would write in an order or notification that you are going to prevent someone or impose some additional checks upon them. It would contain just some normal and usual communication. In addition to the written orders we received, very often, particularly in the period preceding the attack on Srebrenica, orders were conveyed to me that were given orally, that is to say by telephone, from the communications centre, the duty operations officer, and the commander, relating to the convoys, the inspection thereof, and things like that. That is -- please. There was no consistency, let's say, for instance like this: We have received an order. It has to be complied with fully, and there will be no changes thereto. Quite the contrary. There were lots of changes to the orders based on my request for further clarification as to what I'm supposed to do. For instance, if a written order says that the entry is granted, but then we receive an oral order to stop it. Once it reaches Zuti Most we receive an oral order to stop it there. We halt the convoy. Then I phone back and ask, "What am I supposed to do next? I have a written order from the Main Staff that it has to be granted entry without any problems and then in the meantime I receive different orders." So there were lots of misunderstandings and miscommunication and I did my best to cope with the situation, but in 99 per cent of cases we carried out the orders given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's time for the break, madam, if it's convenient for you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question on this topic. I would prefer to put the question now if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If my colleagues agree. Please proceed with your additional question, and then we'll break afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you would receive these changes with regard to the orders, you did not know who was at the origin of this change. The change could have stemmed from the organ of coordination, it could have stemmed from President Karadzic, Mladic, Ivanovic. You cannot tell us who was making these changes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll resume in 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 22nd of April you spoke of a dinner that took place in June 1995 at the Fontana Hotel. Colonel Kingori took part in it. Is it true that Colonel Kingori needed an authorisation in order to be allowed out of Srebrenica to go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. What kind of permit or authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did Colonel Kingori -- did he travel freely in and out of Bratunac, or did he need an approval, an authorisation in order to cross the Zuti Most check-point?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever went out of the Srebrenica enclave, whether it be Dutch Battalion or any other international organisations stationed in Srebrenica, required a permit from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, in order to go to Bratunac, Colonel Kingori needed such a permit or authorisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I have a few questions on the notes that you were kind enough to supply to us at the beginning of your testimony last week. First of all, can you confirm that the notes were drafted as part of the preparation for your defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These notes, let me be quite accurate, were an initial foundation of defence case to be prepared by lawyers, giving them instructions as to what they should deal with and what they should prepare. That is something that I gave them at the very beginning without having insight into other documents and that I thought to be important. Of course, at a later stage some other documents received from the OTP were reviewed, but this was an initial basis for my lawyers to work upon and for potential witnesses to be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, speaking of the dinner organised at the Fontana Hotel, the Prosecutor, that was on the 22nd of April, page 32988, the Prosecutor -- and the following page, 989, the Prosecutor asked you whether you remembered an observation about Colonel Vukota Vukovic in the presence of Colonel Kingori. I'd like to show you an excerpt of your notes. This is Exhibit 5D1438, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, am I allowed to use my notes that I have here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but if anyone asks that you make them available, you will need to. If -- because I don't know whether they are the same notes or whether he's got additional notes. These are the same ones we photocopied earlier on when you first started giving evidence last week, aren't they? They're not something new.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the notes. And if you wish to look at them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's the same notes, there's no problem, but anyone can ask to make sure -- can see them to make sure that they are. So Ms. Fauveau, you may proceed. Mr. Nikolic, you may refer to your notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is the part of your notes in which -- or that dealt with -- with the statement by Mr. Kingori. In the meantime, can we move to e-court -- in e-court to the following page, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want to waste time. I'm going to look on the screen, but if there is something disputable, I will compare it with my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see this mention written next to the name, to the Vukovic name? It is indeed a statement allegedly made by Mr. Vukovic to Mr. Kingori, and in between brackets you say it's not exact because Vukovic would never have said such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you wish me to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just seek your observation. Do you maintain what you wrote back then?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as Vukovic Vukota is concerned, I stand by what I say here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 22nd of April, you also mentioned an action in which the 18th Sabotage Division entered through a tunnel into Srebrenica. The 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've probably misspoken. I received a translation saying that it's the 18th Sabotage Division, but I can help you there. These were elements of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and it also refers to members of the Bratunac Brigade, from the 3rd Infantry Battalion. Well, not to complicate things, these were members of the Bratunac Brigade and elements of the 10th Sabotage and Reconnaissance Detachment of the Main Staff, and the action or the operation mentioned here is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It is fair to say that you personally did not take part in the action?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't enter the tunnel or took -- take part in the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you take part in the planning of the action?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. This action had been planned, organised, and directed by Colonel Salapura through the commander of the Sabotage Detachment, Mr. Pelemis. They were both present on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Muslims in Srebrenica knew of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a question. Those who worked in the Sase mines knew about it, because a large number of Muslims from Srebrenica municipality were employed in the Sase mines, and they lived in the village of the same name like the Sase mine, and that is the Sase village populated by Muslims. After 1992 they all moved to Srebrenica. Therefore, I can say that quite a few people who had been living there knew about the existence of this tunnel, but I don't know who you're specifically referring to. If you're referring to the military, they definitely knew about it, including their officers in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Srebrenica sometimes used the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no information about that. I do not rule out the possibility that they entered the tunnel, carried out sabotage actions, et cetera, but I have no solid proof of that, but it was definitely possible that they were using it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said earlier that Srebrenica was not demilitarised and that the Muslim armed forces carried out actions from the enclave towards Serbian territory. It is fair to say that you cannot preclude that some civilian casualties in the enclave were indeed casualties following from Muslim actions in the enclave, fire from Muslim positions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I completely understood you, but I will try to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the civilian casualties on the Serbian side were the consequence -- please, can you be more precise, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it possible that some casualties, civilian -- Muslim civilian casualties in the enclave were the result of some shooting, fire, coming from the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were killing each other?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Maybe not intentionally, but do you agree that this could have happened, that fire was misdirected, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have put a hypothetical question. Therefore, I can give you a hypothetical answer: Anything is possible. But I really don't know of any such instances, but as I say, anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 5D1434, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: While waiting for the document, let me say that you probably have never seen the document. It is a document from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can page 2, the bottom of it, be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As you can see, this is document from the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated 16th of July, 1995, entitled "Information Regarding the Situation in Srebrenica." Can we move to the next page, please. Towards the middle of the page there is a paragraph starting with little 1, and then one with little 2. They mentioned the causes for the fall of Srebrenica as seen by the ABiH. Under item 1, the end of it, mention is made of negotiations between the head of the Srebrenica municipality with the Chetniks. I just want to know this: Did you know of negotiations between the Muslim authorities in Srebrenica and the Serbian authorities? Whether they be civilian or military, that is not specified in this document.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew about these negotiations, and I myself took part in them on several occasions as part of the negotiating team talking to the Muslims with the mediation of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And during the negotiations, did the Muslims from Srebrenica express certain claims?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all put forward claims, the Muslims, the Serbs, the UNPROFOR, the international observers. Everyone had their respective conditions to put forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslim participation in the negotiation was not authorised by the supreme authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. All I can say with surety is that we agreed meetings through UNPROFOR, that I always had authorisation from the Main Staff, the corps command, or any other decision-maker on the Serbian side. However, whether the Muslims had authorisation either from their Supreme Command or the civilian authorities, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I have a few questions on the directive number 7. You know this is the 8th of March, 1995, directive. Is it true to say that when you were in the Bratunac Brigade, you did not have an opportunity to see the directive back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And all you can say today on the directive would be conclusions that you infer from documents, testimony, information you learnt after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm, concerning the directive, that I read it entirely and learned about its content when I received it within the set of documents from the OTP. I'm sorry, just one more thing. Let me be precise. I may have seen this directive in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, but I honestly don't remember seeing it. However, I don't discount the possibility that it was stored in the brigade archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown P3177. This is information from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, dated 4th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that this information predates directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, I can only say that I accept that this information from the Bratunac Brigade was made before the Main Staff's directive. Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke at length about this document, and you saw it, didn't you, when you were in the Bratunac Brigade. This was sent to each and every soldier in the brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This information was first discussed at the meeting of the Bratunac Brigade command, and then it was distributed to all battalion commanders whose obligation was to study it and to familiarise each and every soldier with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And it is certain that there are certain awkward phrasing that is -- phrases, and that is an understatement in this information. Did you ever ask your commander what was the purpose, what was the objective of this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I never asked him anything about the information. That was the information drafted by him. How he did it, why it was drafted, why it contains what it contains, I had no input in its drafting, and I didn't contribute to it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On several occasions already you spoke about the part played by Miroslav Deronjic in the events in and around Srebrenica in July 1995. Let me show you a part that has not yet been introduced in these trial proceedings. This is P4477. This is the statement you made to the Republika Srpska commission in 2004. Page 11 in B/C/S, page 9 in English, please. Right at the beginning of the page you said this: [In English] "The person responsible for the transport of women and children and all people who apply the status of prisoners by their arrival to Potocari (I am referring to the able-bodied men) is the Commissioner for Civilian Affairs, Miroslav Deronjic, who was appointed by the order of Radovan Karadzic personally."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have received as translation is slightly different than what is written here, but the essence is there. There are just slight differences in what I heard through my headphones. The responsible person for transport of women, children, and all people, who by the arrival in Potocari acquired the status of prisoner, in brackets, able-bodied, and I presume it should be men, is civilian affairs commissioner Miroslav Deronjic appointed by the order of Radovan Karadzic personally. The same order stipulates his powers and obligations. This is that I said, and I still stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Let me turn to your notes. This is 5D1438. I would need to see page 6 -- well, page 5 can be shown first. These are the notes you made about the statement by Mr. Dragomir Vasic. I'm interested in the following page where you wrote about what Mr. Vasic said about the meeting at the Fontana Hotel. Based on your notes, Vasic confirmed that in this conversation Mr. Deronjic was the one who spoke most and that Mr. Vasic did not take part in it. He confirmed that Mladic insisted that the people should surrender and should surrender their weapons, and he was interested in the Muslim army. Deronjic spoke the most regarding civilians and evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you share Dragomir Vasic's opinion on the role played by Mr. Deronjic during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said on many occasions in the courtroom today and previously what I thought about the role of Mr. Deronjic and about himself. I can repeat it if you want me to, but I've said it countless times.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You are right. I will not insist on that topic any longer. However, I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 5D1389. This is a document stemming from the security centre, public security centre of Zvornik, signed by Mr. Vasic. In this document, Mr. Vasic requests fuel, and this is to reimburse -- or in exchange of the civilian population of Srebrenica, for the expenses, actually. So what I would like to know is did you know that the security centre of Zvornik gave fuel for the evacuation of the civilian population of Srebrenica and Potocari? Tell us if you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who provided the fuel, and I particularly don't know what they did within the MUP or within the Zvornik security centre. I did see this document before though.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 22nd of April, page 32977 and 32978, you spoke of the bombing of the civilian column going from Srebrenica to Potocari on the 11th of July, 1995. When you were waiting for your trial, you were able to read the various statements made by the DutchBat members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit 5D1438, page 1. Those are your own notes taken following the statement of Peter Boering.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to show us the following page, please. It's at the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: For the first time you wrote on this page the following: You wrote that he did not notice that there was a -- that the fire was open, and in brackets you say he was in the column, and he did not notice it. And in the other statements, they say that the artillery fire was open from the left and right side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What is the question for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that all you know regarding the bombing that would have taken place, all your information comes from the DutchBat statements?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asserted that. I spoke exactly about the fact that the civilians were targeted from the positions of the Bratunac Brigade. I did not speak of any sort of bombing from either the left or the right. I referred to the fire from T-1 tank, from the 2nd Infantry Battalion -- or, rather, from the positions which were ahead of the 2nd Infantry Battalion's position.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was the B1 gun, interpreter's correction. As for the bombing coming from the left or the right of the road, that's not something I referred to. I have information to the effect that shells landed in the immediate vicinity of the UN base. I don't know anything about that though. I don't know who targeted that particular area or when. What I know for a fact is something that I said in my testimony earlier and over the past several days. As for Mr. Boering's statement we can see here, these were notes I made about the statements he gave. I think that there are several statements, and I don't think that there is any difference in the gist of these statements. I was looking for the differences that would be essential, the differences between his first and second and third statement, and that's what I wanted to draw the attention of the Prosecution to. That was the gist of what Mr. Boering stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. On the 21st of April, 2009, you mentioned on page 32945 and 32946 that you learned from Dragan Mirkovic that the murders in Bratunac in the hangar had taken place. Did Dragan Mirkovic tell you if he himself had gone to the hangar? Did he tell you if he saw those bodies himself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I testified about that, too, and that I talked about it in answer to your colleague's questions earlier on, but let me tell you again. I learned about the events in the hangar from Dragan Mirkovic who, at a later date following the end of the Srebrenica operation and the burials and everything else that happened, told me, simply, that he had personally received orders and that he had been summoned by the authorities - and I'm referring to the president of the municipality, president of the Executive Board, and others who represented the municipality - and that they had asked him carry out the classic "asenacija" or the sanitization of the area around the hangar. He told me that the individuals were transported away from the hangar by bus somewhere to the general area of Glogova - I don't know about that bit - and that they were not buried in the common grave in Glogova and that the area around hangar had been cleaned. That is the extent of what I heard there Dragan Mirkovic. His assessment was that there were between 80 and 100 people there. I don't know myself what the truth is. I had never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I know that you've explained all this to us already, but I would like to know if Dragan Mirkovic told you if he himself went to this hangar. Did he -- did he tell you that? Or maybe he didn't tell you anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that he told me that he had been there himself. I don't know. I simply don't know that. I wouldn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 22nd of April you mentioned that men were separated in Potocari. I would like to show you what you noted on page 10 regarding your own notes. It's on page 10, same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness -- could we show, actually, the bottom page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you see where it says "Page 30"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to what I can read after the dash, you wrote: "It is not exact according to my own information. Nobody was separated for any particular reason."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Nobody was separated for no particular reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see that. I continued to maintain that in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, because this is what is being referred to here, I had no knowledge about anyone having been killed in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, and I had no information to the effect that anyone present in the Vuk Karadzic school was separated. I shared my knowledge with you about the hangar. As for the Vuk Karadzic school, I don't have any information to the effect that anybody had been separated or killed in that particular building. I have also testified about this before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you've assisted some Muslim families in Potocari to get on the buses, and these were, let's say, parents of your students?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I assisted one family consisting of father, mother, children, sons, daughters-in-law. In -- a complete family.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you had no intention to do anything bad, to hurt the Muslims in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have any intentions of doing anything to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In those days, in July of 1995 in Potocari and Bratunac, was your behaviour not due to a feeling that you had towards the Muslim population, negative feeling that you may have had towards them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with certainty that I felt no aversion towards the Muslims. I did not hate the Muslims as a people or as individuals who I used to live with before and during the war. I had a negative attitude towards those persons who had done wrong things. I felt sorry for members of my people. I felt sorry for the victims who had fallen among my people, primarily civilians but also soldiers. I had an aversion towards those whom I was certain that they had taken part in murders and other wrong-doings against my people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You pled guilty for crimes against humanity and persecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did anybody explain to you before you pled guilty that the discriminatory intention is a mandatory element of this crime?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My lawyers tried to explain this to me. The extent to which I was able to grasp all of it in the course of that first year is highly debatable. My understanding was I pled guilty to persecutions because this is how I understood it, and I'll explain this to you in a couple of sentences. My understanding was that persecutions were something that definitely did take place in the area, and I'm referring to Bratunac specifically. There were persecutions in -- in all the areas where there was one ethnicity, a majority. What happened in Bratunac was definitely persecutions committed by the Serbs. I, as a member of the Bratunac Brigade, who held the position that I had, regardless of the extent of my participation, I am in part responsible for the fact that people were driven out of the area. However, I never accepted that I had played a crucial role in driving the people out, that I had taken part in the organisation of persecutions or that I had, God forbid, killed anyone. This is something that cannot be imputed to me by anyone. What I pled guilty to was something that I felt I had a part of blame to take upon myself, and I'm referring to persecutions, because I did to a certain extent help further the commission of persecutions through my deeds. Maybe my understanding was not correct, but that was how I saw it at the time when I decided to plead guilty to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only one question. May I put that question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that mean you're finished with your cross-examination or --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, yes, I'm done, Your Honour. I have one question, and then I will be. It's not terribly important, if you will, so we can stop now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue tomorrow just to make sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse and Mr. Krgovic, how much time will you require tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Almost certainly no time whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd hoped to take no more than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we can reconvene tomorrow and plans can be concluded, Mr. Registrar, for the transfer of Mr. Nikolic back to where he came from. Thank you. Have a nice afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of April, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
